title: He Believed in Yahweh, Who Credited It to Him for Righteousness — Stars, Righteousness, Fire
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace be with you. What we watched in the last lesson was a magnificent victory: Abram brought his nephew home, he refused the goods the king of Sodom held out to him, and he gave a tenth to the priest of God Most High. To all appearances, that was the summit of his faith.
And then chapter 15 opens like this: "After these things Yahweh's word came to Abram in a vision, saying …" Which is to say: the chapter we are about to read comes hard on the heels of that summit.

The question this lesson puts to you is this. Is there something you have been asking God for so long that you are now embarrassed to raise it again? So long that when you pray in front of other people you quietly skip that item, because to say it out loud would make you look as though you had no faith?

Let me put the answer up front. God did not begin by explaining why the man had to wait ten years. He simply changed the direction that man's eyes were pointing. And that night, when the covenant was cut, the only one who walked the road of blood was God himself.
1. The First Time the Bible Says "Don't Be Afraid"
Verse 1: "Yahweh's word came to Abram in a vision, saying, 'Don't be afraid, Abram. I am your shield, your exceedingly great reward.'"

Brothers and sisters, "Don't be afraid" — אַל־תִּירָא (*al-tira*) — this is the first time in the whole Bible that these words are spoken to a human being. And they are spoken to a man who has just come home from a victory.

That is worth turning over for a moment. He has just defeated a coalition of four kings with three hundred and eighteen men. He has just turned down an enormous fortune. Seen from the outside, he is standing at the high point of his life. And the first thing God says when he opens his mouth is: don't be afraid.

Why? Because the hours after a victory are very often the most fragile hours a person has. Will those four kings come back for revenge? I turned the king of Sodom down — what happens to me now? Brothers and sisters, the unease that settles on someone after he has done the right thing is very real.

And God gives him two answers. The first: "I am your shield" — מָגֵן (*magen*). Notice something here. In the last chapter Melchizedek said, "Blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand", and that word "delivered", מִגֵּן (*miggen*), comes from the same root as "shield". The second answer: "your exceedingly great reward" — שְׂכָרְךָ (*secharcha*), which literally means "your wages". He has only just pushed away the king of Sodom's payment, and God says to him next: your wages are with me.
God is never in anybody's debt. What you push away for his sake, he makes up himself.
"Don't be afraid" appears here for the first time in the Bible. Why is it said after a victory?

It is worth noticing where this sentence sits. In chapter 14 he has just rescued Lot and just refused the king of Sodom's goods; by any ordinary reckoning he ought to be up on the heights. And yet chapter 15 opens with God saying, "Don't be afraid." A person's low point very often comes not after failure but after success — the thing is finished, the tension drains out, and only then does he discover how tired he is, how empty, how frightened. On top of that, he has just made enemies of several kings, and the reprisal could come at any moment. So the position of this sentence reminds us of two things. First, the spiritual valley very often follows hard on the summit. Second, in days like those, do not hold yourself up alone — those are precisely the days when God intends to speak.
God says, "I am your shield, your exceedingly great reward." What exactly is the reward?

There are two ways of reading the Hebrew, and both are grammatical. One: "I am your shield; your reward will be exceedingly great." The other: "I am your shield, your exceedingly great reward" — that is, God himself is the reward. The second reading fits beautifully with what Abram says next: what he wants is offspring, and what God gives him first is himself. That point is crucial for the way we live our faith: what we ask for is usually God's things, and the first thing God hands over is usually himself. Of course he did in the end give Abram offspring as well; but the order cannot be reversed — a person who wants God's hand and not God's face will still be empty, however large the reward.
2. He Said the True Thing Out Loud
Verse 2: "Abram said, 'Lord Yahweh, what will you give me, since I go childless …'"
Brothers and sisters, stop at that sentence. God has only just said, "I am your exceedingly great reward", and the man's answer is: what is there left that you can give me?

In Hebrew that sentence carries a considerable weight of feeling. The word for "childless", עֲרִירִי (*ariri*), is a heavy word; the sense underneath it is of being stripped, left bare and bald. And then he goes on: "Behold, you have given no children to me: and, behold, one born in my house is my heir."

And here is the irony of it — the steward's name. Eliezer, אֱלִיעֶזֶר (*Eli'ezer*), means "God is help". With one breath he complains that God has not helped him, and with the same breath he points at a man whose name is "God is help".

There is one more detail. This is the first place in the Bible where the compound title "Lord Yahweh", אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה (*Adonai YHWH*), appears. The tone of it is reverent and close at the same time — he has not been rude, and he has said every word that was in his heart.
Brothers and sisters, I want you to notice how God responds. God does not rebuke him. God does not say, "How can you speak to me like that", and God does not say, "Where has your faith gone?"

For pastoral work this matters enormously. Something close to a third of the Psalms are laments — prayers with no conclusion, no tidy structure, nothing in them but pain. The first line of Psalm 13 is, "How long, Yahweh? Will you forget me forever?" God gathered prayers like that into his own book.

A church that will not let people say the true thing does not, in the end, raise up people of faith. It raises up people who are very good at pretending. And once a person begins to pretend in God's presence, he drifts further and further from God — because now he has to filter himself before he dares to pray at all.
So hear this clearly: the first spiritual thing Abram did that day was to say out loud the sentence he had not dared to say.
Abram says straight out to God, "You have given no children to me." Is it all right to complain like that?

Scripture writes that conversation down exactly as it happened, and God does not rebuke him. In fact the Old Testament is full of conversations like it — a great many of the Psalms are laments, and the whole book of Habakkuk is one long interrogation. That is an enormous release for us: the true thing can be carried into God's presence. What needs watching is the direction the complaint faces. Abram spoke *to* God; he was not talking *about* God. The first carries the trouble into the relationship; the second discusses it from outside the relationship. The practical test is very simple: that sentence of yours — do you say it when you pray, or only when you are chatting with other people? Say it to God once, and you will find that the sentence begins to have a way out.
God told him to count the stars — but that was at night. What about the daytime? Do I have to see something before I can go on believing?

God really did give him a picture he could see, and that tells us God makes allowance for our weakness — he does not mind that we need something to hold on to. But notice what verse 6 says: "He believed in Yahweh." The object of the faith is that person, not those stars. Stars can be covered by cloud; that person cannot. So the healthy practice is this: receive every visible sign God gives you — a verse, an astonishing provision, a person who turned up at exactly the right moment — but put the weight of your faith on the one who is speaking. In practice you can write down the signs God has already given you, and on the days when you can see nothing, take the list out and read it. That is not superstition. That is what people with poor memories ought to do.
3. A Light from the Original: "Credited" Is a Bookkeeper's Word
Verse 5: "Yahweh brought him outside, and said, 'Look now toward the sky, and count the stars, if you are able to count them.' He said to Abram, 'So your offspring will be.'"
Brothers and sisters, God does not answer the question "why must I wait ten years?" He does something else instead: he takes the man outside and tells him to lift his head.

Inside the tent, what he could see was an old man with no children. Outside, with his head tilted back, what he could see was a sky full of stars. The same circumstances, the same man — turn his eyes in another direction and the weight of the thing is no longer the same.
And at that moment he did not yet have a single child. God showed a whole sky of stars to a man with no son.
And then comes verse 6, one of the most important verses in the whole Bible: "He believed in Yahweh, who credited it to him for righteousness."
The word behind "credited" is וַיַּחְשְׁבֶהָ (*vayachsheveha*), from the root חָשַׁב (*chashav*). It is a bookkeeper's word: to enter a figure in somebody's account.

Brothers and sisters, this has to be said very plainly. Romans 4:4–5 says, "Now to him who works, the reward is not counted as grace, but as something owed. But to him who doesn't work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is accounted for righteousness." Paul says it outright: this is not wages. This is grace.

So "faith" here is not a merit, and the verse does not mean "he believed strongly enough, so God handed him a prize". Faith is the channel, not the condition. The righteousness was entered in the ledger — and the one keeping the books is God.

And notice where this verse stands in time. It happens before the circumcision of chapter 17, and before the offering of Isaac in chapter 22. Romans 4 builds its whole argument on exactly that gap: justification does not rest on a rite, and it does not rest on a record of performance. When Paul wants to prove that a person is justified by faith, the verse he reaches for is Genesis 15:6.

Then what, brothers and sisters, are we to do with James 2:24, which says, "You see then that by works a man is justified, and not only by faith"? Notice what James is pointing at: he is pointing at the offering of Isaac in chapter 22, and he says, "So the Scripture was fulfilled which says, 'Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him as righteousness.'" Paul is speaking about the root of justification; James is speaking about the evidence of justification. Paul is arguing against people who try to earn it by works; James is arguing against people who can talk and cannot act. The two apostles are fighting two different battles — and the order between them cannot be inverted: first the root, then the fruit.
"Credited it to him for righteousness" — what does that word "credited" actually mean?

The Hebrew חָשַׁב (*chashav*) is an act of bookkeeping: registering a sum in a particular account. So what this verse says is that Abram did not produce righteousness — God entered righteousness in his account. Paul quotes this verse in both Romans 4 and Galatians 3 as the most basic Old Testament ground for justification by faith, and he presses one point especially hard: it happened before Abram was circumcised and before the law was given. So the order of salvation has never once changed since the beginning: first you believe, then it is credited to you as righteousness, and only after that come the signs and the works. The reason you can stand before God today is not that your balance is large enough. It is that somebody made the deposit for you.
4. The Only One Who Walked the Road of Blood Was God Himself
In verse 7 God says, "I am Yahweh who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldees, to give you this land to inherit it." And in verse 8 Abram asks, "Lord Yahweh, how will I know that I will inherit it?"
Brothers and sisters, in verse 6 he has only just believed, and by verse 8 he is asking, "How will I know?" Is that unbelief?

I do not think it is. Set it beside Luke 1. Zacharias asks, "How can I be sure of this? For I am an old man, and my wife is well advanced in years", and he is rebuked for it. Mary asks, "How can this be, seeing I am a virgin?", and the angel simply explains it to her. The same form of question — and what decides the matter is the heart behind it. And God's response to Abram is not a rebuke. It is a covenant.

Verse 9: "He said to him, 'Bring me a heifer three years old, a female goat three years old, a ram three years old, a turtledove, and a young pigeon.'" Verse 10: "He brought him all these, and divided them in the middle, and laid each half opposite the other."

Brothers and sisters, this is the ancient Near Eastern ceremony of "cutting" a covenant. Jeremiah 34:18–19 records the same procedure: the two parties to the covenant walk between the divided pieces, and what the walk means is this — if I break this covenant, let me become like these animals.
So by the rules of the ceremony, what should happen next is that Abram and God walk between the pieces together.
But verse 12 says, "When the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell on Abram. Now terror and great darkness fell on him."
He fell asleep. The word for "deep sleep" is תַּרְדֵּמָה (*tardemah*), and the last time it appeared was in 2:21, when God put the man to sleep. The human being sleeps; God goes to work.
Then verse 17: "It came to pass that, when the sun went down, and it was dark, behold, a smoking furnace and a flaming torch passed between these pieces."

Brothers and sisters, only one party made that walk. A smoking furnace and a flaming torch — those are signs of the presence of God, and the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire at the exodus later draw on the very same imagery.
God walked that road of blood alone. Which is to say: if this covenant is ever broken, the price will be paid by him.

And thousands of years later, at Golgotha, that price really was paid. Human beings did not keep this covenant — not once, not ever. And God, according to the oath he swore that night as he passed between the pieces, handed himself over. The reason your salvation is secure is that when this covenant was signed, there was only one signature on it.
God told Abram to cut the animals in half. What does that way of making a covenant mean?

It is the covenant ceremony of the ancient Near East: the animals are cut in two, and the parties to the covenant walk between the halves, which says, "If I break this covenant, may I become like these animals." Jeremiah 34 records Israel making a covenant in exactly that way. And here is the most astonishing thing in chapter 15: Abram is asleep, and the text says that "a smoking furnace and a flaming torch passed between these pieces" — the only one who walked through was God. Which means that both sides of the obligation in this covenant were carried by God alone. This is precisely the announcement of the cross in advance: we are the ones who break the covenant, and he is the one who walks the road of blood. Which is why this covenant cannot be voided by our failure.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first is to preach "credited it to him for righteousness" as though faith were a merit. It gets preached like this: he believed well enough, and so God rewarded him. Romans 4 goes out of its way to insist that the righteousness was *credited* to him, not earned as wages for work done. Preach it as a merit and you have swapped grace for a transaction, and the congregation will go home and start adding up their own scores.

The second is to preach Abram's complaint as a failure he ought never to have had. A preacher reaches verse 2 and hurries to add, "Of course, we should never question God like this." But God did not rebuke him. God took him outside instead. If a church will not let people say the true thing, people will simply back away from God very politely.

The third is to take the four-hundred-year prophecy and use it to work out a modern timetable. Verses 13 to 16 are an announcement about that stretch of history; they are not a formula for calculating dates in our own day. Any teaching that sets people counting days has walked away from what the text is for. As for the four hundred years here and the four hundred and thirty years of Exodus 12:40, that is a question of different starting points, and we handle it separately in the map of disputed questions.

The fourth is to preach the romance of counting stars and never to preach the animals cut in half. That bloody ceremony in verses 9 to 17 is where the whole weight of God's faithfulness rests. Preach only the night sky and this chapter shrinks into a line of encouragement. What the congregation ought to carry home is the God who walked the road of blood alone — not only the stars overhead.

The fifth is to preach "the iniquity of the Amorite is not yet full" as though God were standing by with cold eyes. What that line in verse 16 says is that God's patience has a measure to it — he would rather wait another four generations than move early. 2 Peter 3:9 tells us that he is patient, not wishing that anyone should perish. So this verse is a comfort and a warning at the same time: the person you have been praying for — God has more patience with him than you have; and the period of forbearance has a length to it.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question. Chinese people are taught from childhood to report the good news and keep the bad news to ourselves, and we carry that habit straight into God's presence — in prayer we dare to give thanks and we do not dare to complain, because complaining feels irreverent. Is that right? Brothers and sisters, this chapter gives a very direct answer: Abram said the ugliest sentence he had in him, and God's response was to lead him outside to look at the stars. Psalm 142:2 says, "I pour out my complaint before him. I tell him my troubles." The word behind "pour out" carries the sense of tipping a vessel over and emptying it. So telling the truth in God's presence is not irreverence; it is the evidence of a relationship — the only people you say ugly things to are the people you are genuinely close to. But let me add one balancing word: saying the true thing is not the same as losing your temper. What Abram put into words was his situation and his bewilderment; he was not accusing God of injustice. You may say, "I don't understand", "I am in pain", "I cannot wait any longer" — God receives every one of those.

The second question. An elder in the family says, "Store up merit, do good, and heaven will look after you" — how is that different from justification by faith? Here is how I would suggest you talk about it. First, affirm what is true: doing good is a good thing in itself, and the whole Bible calls people to do justice and to love mercy. Second, name the difference: the logic of storing up merit is "I put in so much, and I get so much back" — it is a ledger; whereas Genesis 15:6 says that righteousness was *credited*, entered by God in the man's account. Third, push the question down to the most practical layer of all — if you live by storing up merit, how long must you go on storing before it counts as enough? Who is going to tell you that you have done enough? Brothers and sisters, that is the deepest pain of merit-keeping: it never issues the declaration "enough". And that declaration is precisely what the gospel gives — "It is finished." So you might put it like this: you taught me to do good, and I will be grateful to you all my life; it is only that later on I found I could never know whether I had done enough — until someone said "enough" on my behalf.
God says the offspring "will live as foreigners in a land that is not theirs" for four hundred years. Why is there so hard a stretch inside a promise?

This verse reminds us that hardship is included in God's promise; it is not a sign that the promise has gone wrong. And God says the hard part plainly in advance — he does not trick anybody into getting on board. In the same speech he also gives three guarantees: "I will also judge that nation, whom they will serve"; "you will go to your fathers in peace. You will be buried at a good old age"; "In the fourth generation they will come here again." So the hardship has a term, a purpose and an outcome. That is very practical for us: when you are inside a stretch of days whose end you cannot see, you may ask God for one of those three — a term, a meaning, or a picture of how it ends. With one of them in your hand, you can hold on.
7. Living 321 Out — Letting Him Decide Where I Look
Brothers and sisters, let us tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — God put Abram into a deep sleep and walked that road of blood himself. And when the Lord Jesus prayed alone in Gethsemane, the disciples were asleep; when he hung on the cross, the disciples had scattered. Brothers and sisters, my role model is this: he walked, in my place, the stretch of road I could not walk. That is not a figure of speech. This chapter is the picture of it.

The Bible is my standard — this chapter hands us one of the most fundamental standards there is: righteousness is credited, not earned. Once that standard is settled in you, the whole centre of gravity of your faith shifts — from "have I performed well enough today?" to "he has already entered it in my account." And that shift decides whether you live in freedom or live inside a performance review.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — look at the action in verse 5: "Yahweh brought him outside." Guidance is sometimes not the handing over of an answer; it is a change of position. The problem you have been turning over and cannot think your way through may not need more analysis at all. It may need somebody to lead you outside and tell you to lift your head.

Let Jesus be King — with the focus on myself, what I see is an old man with no children; with the focus on God, what I see is the Lord who can number the stars. To let Jesus be King is to let him decide where I look. Brothers and sisters, this happens every single day: when you open your eyes in the morning, is the first thing you look at the bad news on your phone, or the one who made the constellations?

Let Jesus receive all the glory — in the covenant ceremony of this chapter the man does exactly three things: he cuts the animals in half, he drives off the birds of prey, and then he falls asleep. Through the decisive part of it he was asleep. That is what grace looks like — the most important part is not the part you completed.

Establish God's system — in verses 13 to 16 God tells the whole story of the exodus before it happens: four hundred years living as foreigners, serving, being afflicted, and then coming out with great wealth. Brothers and sisters, his plans are measured in units of four hundred years. So to establish God's system you have to look at time on his scale and not on mine. A person who assesses the work of God by the quarterly report will be disappointed again and again.

And here I want to say something honest about 321 itself. We stress that when the mindset changes the life changes — and this chapter reminds us that Abram's mindset was already right in verse 6: he believed, and it was credited to him as righteousness. And then in chapter 16 he goes along with Sarai and uses a human method. So the renewing of the mindset is necessary, and it is not finished in a single stroke. Faith is not a switch; it is a road. In pastoral work, give people the length of that road, and do not take one confession of faith and demand a lifetime of steadiness on the strength of it.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One and the Same Sky of Stars
Brothers and sisters, one and the same sky of stars falls into four different kinds of heart — and what each of them sees is not the same.

The proud heart sees how good its own faith is. This heart reads verse 6 and thinks: I am going to become a person of faith like Abraham. Brothers and sisters, look carefully — the leading figure in that verse is not his faith. It is the God who keeps the books. Once faith turns into an achievement, it has stopped being faith.

The fearful heart sees this: "Is my faith enough?" This heart checks its own feelings over and over, and reasons that if there is no sense of assurance while it prays, that must mean it has not believed enough. To a heart like that I want to say: the weight of faith does not lie in how strong your emotions are. It lies in who you have put the whole weight on. A thin cord tied to a solid pillar is far safer than a thick rope tied to a rotten post. The point is not the rope. The point is the pillar.

The ashamed heart sees this: "Somebody like me, who still complains — I probably do not count as a person of faith at all." Brothers and sisters, read verse 2 and verse 6 side by side. The man who said, "What will you give me?", and the man who "believed in Yahweh" and had it credited to him as righteousness, are the same man — and it was the same day. God did not delete the complaint from the record, and he did not withhold the credit because of it.

The wounded heart sees this: "He gave Abram a child — so what about the thing I have been asking for?" You may have been asking for many years, and the thing has never happened. Brothers and sisters, I am not going to hand you a cheap answer. I only ask you to look at two things. First, what Abram received in this chapter was not a child; it was a covenant — the child was another fourteen years away. Second, Hebrews 11:13 says of these people that they "all died in faith, not having received the promises". Scripture never pretends that every waiting is honoured within this life. And the hope it gives is longer than this life.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, say once the sentence you have not dared to say. Find a stretch of time when nobody is around, and tell God the whole of it exactly as it stands — that matter you have prayed about for years and are now embarrassed to mention. No polishing. No adding, "Of course I know God's timing is best." That is how Abram began that night.

Second, go outside. Actually go out — find a place where you can see the sky, and stand there for three minutes. The first prescription God gave Abram was not an explanation. It was a change of place and a lifted head.

Third, write the crediting down. Take a piece of paper and write: "My righteousness is not something I earned; it is something he entered in my account." Put it somewhere you will see it every day, and leave it there for seven days. Every time you accuse yourself this week, go and look at that sentence.

Fourth, look at your trouble once on a four-hundred-year scale. Write down the thing you are most anxious about at the moment, and then write beside it: if God works in units of four hundred years, whereabouts on his calendar might this thing be sitting?

Fifth, this week tell this lesson to one friend outside the church, in three sentences. There is a man in the Bible who waited ten years for a child and then said straight out to God, "What is there left that you can give me?" — and God did not rebuke him; he simply led him outside to look at the stars. Then Scripture says, "He believed in Yahweh, who credited it to him for righteousness" — and that word "credited" is a bookkeeper's word: righteousness was entered in his account, it was not earned by him. And that night, when the covenant was cut, the rules said both parties should walk between the halves of the animals — but the man fell asleep, and the only one who walked through was God himself.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that my righteousness is not something I earned; it is something God credited to my account.
I declare that I will say the true thing in God's presence; he has room for my bewilderment, and room for my pain.
I declare that I let him decide where I look; I will stop staring at my own empty hands, and I will lift my head.
I declare that the price of this covenant was paid by him, and therefore my salvation stands secure.
This week I am to "bring the true thing to God" — but I am afraid that saying it out loud would be irreverent. What should I do?

Look first at what Scripture itself does. Moses said, "Why have you treated your servant so badly?" Job said, "I will tell God, 'Do not condemn me.'" Jeremiah said, "Yahweh, you have persuaded me, and I was persuaded" — and the Hebrew verb there, פִּתִּיתַנִי (*pittitani*), is the word used elsewhere for enticing or seducing someone. And the Lord Jesus on the cross quoted a psalm: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" God gathered every one of those sentences into his own book. So irreverence is not saying the true thing; irreverence is saying the false thing — playing, in prayer, a person you are not. In practice: find a quiet stretch of time, write that sentence down, read it out loud, and at the end add one more line — "Lord, I still mean to trust you." You will find that once it has been said, the weight of that sentence grows lighter.
Brothers and sisters, if only one picture from this lesson may remain, let it be that torch moving through the darkness.

The sun is going down. An old man has fallen into a deep sleep, and a terror and a great darkness have come down on him. The animals lie on the ground, cut in half, and the smell of blood is still in the air. And through that darkness a smoking furnace and a flaming torch move, between the pieces, all the way through.

Brothers and sisters, the darkness of that night was not an accident. Behind every great promise God gives, there is a price that God himself pays. When we say lightly, "this is the grace of God", do not forget the darkness of that night — grace has never once been cheap.

And notice how the whole thing is finally settled. Galatians 3:13–14 says, "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us … that the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles through Christ Jesus."
When God walked the road of blood that night, he already knew where the price would fall. And knowing it completely, he walked through.

So the reason that line in verse 6 — "He believed in Yahweh" — is able to stand is not that his believing was so fine. It is that the one he believed in is a God who will walk into the darkness for the sake of a covenant.

The focus is not on how great my faith is, not on how long I have waited, and not on whether I feel any assurance today. The focus is on Jesus — he is the Lord who passed between the pieces and then went up to the cross. Not I, but Christ.

May God bless every one of us this week: to dare to say that true sentence out loud, and then to walk outside, lift our heads, and count a few of his stars. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at a mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★ The first "Don't be afraid" in the Bible comes after a victory. What is that timing reminding us of?
2. ★★★ The word behind "credited it to him for righteousness" is an act of bookkeeping. How does that change your anxiety about whether you are good enough?
3. ★ Abram said something very blunt to God, and God did not rebuke him. What difference does that make to the way you pray?
4. ★★ When the covenant was cut, the only one who walked between the pieces was God. What does that picture say?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I do not need a guarantee), fearful (more frightened after the success than before it), ashamed (I dare not say the true thing to God), wounded (I once asked for a long time and never received it). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "He believed in Yahweh, who credited it to him for righteousness." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Is there a "not yet" sentence inside you that you have never dared to say to God? You do not have to say what it is. Only say this: what is it that stops you saying it out loud?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "The thing I have always wanted God to give me is …"
9. ★★ This week, in what way will you bring that true sentence to God? Name the time, the place and the manner.

Leader's reminder: question seven will touch prayers that have gone unanswered for years. Do not explain on God's behalf why he has not given it yet, and never say, "Your faith isn't strong enough." Stay with the person first and let him finish saying what he has to say.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your own home, is there someone who has been waiting a long time for something? How will you keep him company this week?
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work or at school, who is gritting his teeth and holding on?
12. ★★★ The star-counting practice: this week write down three signs God has given you in the past, and put them up somewhere you can see them. Say now where you will put them.
13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — and tell him first the thing you wanted to say in question nine and did not dare to say. Say his name now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First, there is a man in the Bible who said straight out to God, "You have not given me anything yet." Second, God did not rebuke him; he took him outside to count the stars instead. Third, so I believe in a God who can take the true thing from me. Write down now who you will tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the one true sentence you will say to God this week, and the one person you will keep company. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord that while we still cannot see, we would go on putting the whole weight on him.
